distinctions.name: Two senses of ‘more fundamental’

left.label: Whole prior to parts (for understanding)
left.desc: We understand a part by its role in the whole: a leg is for moving about, an eye for seeing, a book cover for protecting the pages, a cushion for comfort.

right.label: Parts prior to whole (for existence)
right.desc: The whole cannot exist unless its parts exist and are arranged the right way; heap them up, scatter them, or build a table instead and the chair is gone.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument runs on the second sense. Seeing both keeps you from caricaturing it as treating wholes as mere heaps; it grants the whole's priority for understanding while noting that the whole's being depends on its parts' union.

distinctions.name: Temporal vs. atemporal dependence

left.label: Temporal (historical)
left.desc: The parts existed first and were later assembled, as with a manufactured chair. True of some composites but not all — a body's organs develop together.

right.label: Atemporal (moment by moment)
right.desc: At every moment it exists, a composite needs its parts united at that moment — whether it was assembled, grew, appeared all at once, or always existed.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Because the argument uses atemporal dependence, it is untouched by debates over whether the universe had a beginning, and it concludes to a cause operating now rather than merely long ago.

distinctions.name: Linear vs. hierarchical causes of a composite

left.label: Linear (per accidens)
left.desc: The worker who assembled the chair; he can retire or die and the chair stays put. For all this argument cares, such a series could stretch back forever.

right.label: Hierarchical (per se)
right.desc: Screws, friction, molecular and atomic bonds, suitable temperature: each contributes only what it derives from deeper factors, and all must be at work for the chair to exist now.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only a hierarchical series must have a first member. That is what forces the regress to end in something with underived existence — which must then be partless.

distinctions.name: Physical vs. metaphysical parts

left.label: Physical (integral) parts
left.desc: Pieces you could in principle point to or separate: legs, screws, pages, organs, molecules, atoms.

right.label: Metaphysical parts (principles)
right.desc: Distinct but inseparable principles that together make up a concrete thing: form and matter, essence and existence, actuality and potentiality, a bearer and its features.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The One must lack both. Something with no physical parts (a soul, an angel) could still be metaphysically composite and so still need a cause. Absolute simplicity is far stronger than mere immateriality.

distinctions.name: ‘Everything has a cause’ vs. ‘Whatever is composite has a cause’

left.label: What critics attack
left.desc: An exceptionless principle that everything whatsoever has a cause — which would indeed demand a cause for God.

right.label: What the argument says
right.desc: Only what has parts needs a cause of their union; what is absolutely simple neither needs nor could have one.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This dissolves ‘What caused God?’. God is not a special-pleading exception; the principle simply does not apply to what has no parts, much as ‘all triangles have three sides’ says nothing about circles.

distinctions.name: Sense vs. reference

left.label: Sense
left.desc: The way an expression presents its object; its meaning. ‘The One is omnipotent’ and ‘the One is an intellect’ differ in sense.

right.label: Reference
right.desc: The object an expression picks out. ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ both pick out Venus.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It shows how many true, non-synonymous descriptions of God (powerful, intelligent, eternal) can all be about one simple reality without introducing parts into it.

distinctions.name: Univocal vs. analogical predication (with equivocal as the other extreme)

left.label: Univocal
left.desc: Same sense in both uses: ‘dog’ said of Rover and of Fido. (At the opposite extreme, equivocal use has wholly unrelated senses: ‘bat’ for the club and the animal.)

right.label: Analogical
right.desc: Related but not identical senses: ‘good’ said of wine and of George. Still literal, not metaphorical.

distinctions.whyItMatters: If ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ applied to God exactly as they do to us, they would name distinct features — parts. Used analogically, they say there is something in God corresponding to each, while in him they are one.

distinctions.name: An alternative explanation vs. no explanation

left.label: Alternative explanation
left.desc: A rival account of why the parts are united (a further part? the laws of nature?), which must then be assessed on its merits — and each such account regenerates the problem.

right.label: No explanation (brute fact)
right.desc: Simply declaring that the union of the parts has no explanation at all.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Critics often present ‘it's just a brute fact’ as though it competed with the Neo-Platonic explanation. It doesn't; it declines to explain. With an explanation on the table and no non-question-begging reason to reject it, ‘maybe there's no explanation’ is not a serious reply.

illustrations.title: The chair you are sitting on
illustrations.body:
Feser's central example. Your chair has legs, screws, a frame, a seat, a cushion. Pile those pieces in the corner, or bolt them together as a small table, and you no longer have a chair: the chair needs its parts to exist *and* to be arranged a certain way.

Now ask what keeps them arranged right now. Screws hold the legs to the frame; friction keeps the screws in place; the wood and metal hold together because their molecules are bonded, and the molecules because their atoms are. Even the room's temperature is doing work: make it hot enough and the screws melt and the wood burns. At every moment the chair exists, a whole stack of factors must be combined just so. The chair contributes none of this to itself.

illustrations.title: The body that was never assembled, and the chair that always existed
illustrations.body: One might think ‘dependence on parts’ just means ‘was put together at some time’. Feser blocks this with two cases. Your body was never assembled from ready-made arms and eyes; the organs all developed together as cells divided in the womb. And imagine a chair that had existed forever, or one that popped into being all at once. In every case the thing still depends, at each moment, on its parts existing and being united at that moment. The dependence the argument cares about is about *now*, not about the past.

illustrations.title: Copper, trees, and animals: one form, many things
illustrations.body: Why are three separate lumps all copper rather than lead or gold? For the Aristotelian, because they share one and the same form, which gives them malleability and conductivity. Likewise every tree shares the form of tree (drawing up water through roots) and every animal the form of animal (sensing through organs). What makes this lump a different copper *thing* from that one is its matter. But the form apart from matter is only an abstraction, and matter apart from form is only a potential to be something. Neither can supply the union of the two, so even at this deep metaphysical level the thing needs a cause of its composition.

illustrations.title: The triangle: what it is and that it is
illustrations.body: The essence of triangle — a closed plane figure with three straight sides — is shared by every triangle, while each triangle has its own existence. You never meet a triangle's existence without its being a triangle; and the essence on its own, belonging to no actual triangle, is just an abstraction. So in any concrete triangle, essence and existence lean on each other, and something outside the triangle must account for their being joined. Feser uses this to show that the composition principle applies even to parts no microscope could reveal.

illustrations.title: The glue that needs glue
illustrations.body: Feser, following Vallicella, considers the suggestion that one part of a thing unites the others. Picture two boards, A and B, joined by glue, C. What joins the glue to the boards, and holds the glue itself together? Posit a further binder D, and you must ask what joins D to A, B, and C. Each new ‘unifier’ is just another part that needs unifying. Adding parts never explains unity; it only lengthens the list of things to be unified.

illustrations.title: The morning star and the evening star
illustrations.body: Ancient observers named a bright light in the dawn sky and a bright light in the evening sky as if they were two things. ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ really do mean different things — each phrase presents its object differently — but both refer to one planet, Venus. Feser uses Frege's example to show that ‘the One's power’ and ‘the One's intellect’ can differ in meaning while referring to one simple reality. Many descriptions do not entail many parts.

illustrations.title: Good wine and a good man
illustrations.body: Call a dog ‘a dog’ and another dog ‘a dog’ and you use the word the same way (univocally). Call a club a ‘bat’ and a flying mammal a ‘bat’ and the meanings have nothing to do with each other (equivocally). But say the wine is good and George is good, and the meanings are neither identical nor unrelated: the wine's goodness and George's goodness are analogous. No metaphor is involved; both are literally good. This is how, following Aquinas, we should speak of God's goodness, power, and intellect.

illustrations.title: Wave–particle duality
illustrations.body: Physics tells us that electrons and photons behave in some ways like particles and in some ways like waves. Nobody can picture that well, yet the evidence and theory compel it — and we should *expect* difficulty, because we are stretching concepts built for tables and pebbles to cover things far beyond everyday experience. Feser argues that the ground of all reality is farther still from everyday experience, so it would be suspicious if our concepts did *not* strain when applied to it. Difficulty of comprehension is a predicted feature of the conclusion, not evidence against it.

illustrations.title: The army and the chorus (Plotinus)
illustrations.body: Plotinus liked to point out that an army, a chorus, or a flock exists as such only while it has unity. Disband the army and the soldiers still exist, but the army is gone; scatter the singers and there is no chorus. The same holds for a house or a living body. His conclusion: being and unity go together, every many presupposes a one, and so the source of all things must be unity itself. Feser's chair argument is a modern, step-by-step version of this ancient insight.

illustrations.title: The magnetic sculpture
illustrations.body:
Imagine a sculpture of loose steel pieces that stays standing only because an electromagnet in its base is switched on. Nothing in the sculpture holds the sculpture together; cut the current and it collapses at once — even if it had stood there forever. The magnet in turn works only because current flows from a generator, which runs only because something else drives it. Each level holds only because something deeper holds it.

Use this to show: (1) atemporal dependence (the sculpture's unity must be sustained now); (2) the further-part mistake (pointing to one steel piece as ‘the holder’ just adds a piece that also needs holding); (3) the hierarchy (borrowed holding-power at every level). And mark where the analogy breaks: the One is not one more physical power source at the bottom of the stack, but the partless ground on which every level, including the laws of electromagnetism, depends.

objections.title: “Even if there's a first cause, why call it God?”
objections.whoRaises: Popular skeptics; a common reaction to any cosmological argument
objections.objection: Grant, for argument's sake, that composite things trace back to something simple. That is a far cry from God. The ultimate cause might be an impersonal force, a physical field, or something we have no name for. Jumping from ‘first cause’ to the God of theism is wishful thinking.
objections.reply:
Feser answers that this objection is lazy in the context of this argument, because Stage 2 gives specific reasons for each divine attribute.

- It must be **unique**, because two simple things could differ only by a feature one has and the other lacks — which would make them composite.
- It must be **changeless and eternal**, because change, beginning, and ending all require parts.
- It is **not physical**, because physical things have parts; **not abstract**, because abstractions cause nothing; **not a mental content**, because thoughts depend on minds. So it is a **mind**.
- It must be **purely actual**, since a mix of act and potency is a composition; and from pure actuality chapter 1 derives perfection, omnipotence, goodness, and omniscience.

One may criticize any of those steps (and chapter 6 takes up such criticisms), but one cannot simply assert that the cause need not be divine.
objections.pushback: If the objector says ‘an impersonal field could be simple,’ ask whether a field has parts or structure, varies from place to place, has values it could lack, or could have been otherwise. Any of these makes it composite. If they say ‘fine, but maybe your attribute arguments fail,’ agree that this is the right place for the debate — and ask which specific step they reject.

objections.title: “The argument assumes the universe had a beginning”
objections.whoRaises: Critics familiar with the kalām argument; anyone who hears ‘first cause’ as ‘earliest cause’
objections.objection: Arguments like this depend on tracing causes back to a first moment. But modern cosmology leaves open that the universe (or a multiverse) is past-eternal. If there was no first moment, there is no first cause.
objections.reply: The argument makes no claim about a first moment. Its dependence is **atemporal**: at any moment a composite exists, it needs its parts united at that moment. Feser explicitly says that even an everlasting chair would depend on its parts. The regress is not traced backward in time to a beginning but downward, here and now, to a cause that is sustaining things at this very moment. The word ‘first’ means ‘ultimate, underived’, not ‘earliest’. So the argument goes through whether the universe is past-eternal or not.
objections.pushback: If they insist that every causal argument is secretly about time, walk through the chair in a heated room: whether or not the chair has existed forever, it would fall apart *now* if the conditions sustaining it failed now. That's the kind of dependence at issue.

objections.title: “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”
objections.whoRaises: Bertrand Russell's lineage; Richard Dawkins and many popular writers
objections.objection: The argument says things need causes. Then God needs a cause too. If God can be uncaused, why not the universe? Either way, calling God the exception is special pleading.
objections.reply: The argument never says everything has a cause. Its premise is that **whatever is composite** needs a cause of its composition. God is not an arbitrary exception: something absolutely simple has nothing to be put together, so it not only needs no cause but *could not* have one. Nor is this a dodge invented to escape the objection; it was the point of the Neo-Platonic tradition from the start. And the universe cannot play God's role, because the universe is massively composite. Feser concludes that the objection, far from devastating, completely misses the target.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘you just defined God as uncaused,’ reply that simplicity was not stipulated; it was argued for (steps 6–8): any composite cause would need a further cause, so the regress can only end in something partless. The uncausedness then follows from the partlessness. If they say ‘then the universe could be simple,’ ask how something with galaxies, particles, and changing states could lack parts.

objections.title: Hume and quantum mechanics: things can exist without causes
objections.whoRaises: David Hume; appeals to quantum indeterminacy (e.g., Victor Stenger)
objections.objection: Hume showed we can conceive of something existing without a cause, so causal principles aren't necessary truths. And quantum mechanics shows that some events happen without causes. So why believe every composite needs a cause of its composition?
objections.reply:
Feser refers the reader back to his replies in chapter 1, which apply equally here. In brief:

- Imagining something appearing without *also imagining* its cause is not conceiving of it as having *no* cause — just as thinking of a trilateral without thinking ‘triangle’ doesn't show a trilateral could fail to be a triangle.
- Experience overwhelmingly supports causal principles: we find causes when we look, and things don't pop into being at random.
- Quantum indeterminism at most shows some events lack *deterministic* causes, not that they lack causes; quantum systems still have structure and conditions.

Applied to this chapter: even an electron in a quantum state is something whose features and constituents must actually be joined for it to exist. Indeterminacy about what it will do next doesn't show that its existence right now needs no ground.
objections.pushback: If they press that the principle is merely an empirical generalization that could fail, note that the composition premise is not a claim about sequences of events but about what it is to be a whole: a whole just is its parts-united, and a union of distinct items is not self-explanatory. Ask them to describe a case where a thing's parts are united without anything accounting for it — not merely without *us* knowing what does.

objections.title: Many attributes mean many parts
objections.whoRaises: Critics of divine simplicity; thoughtful students on first hearing
objections.objection: The argument ends by listing a dozen attributes: omnipotence, intellect, goodness, eternity, and so on. But having many distinct attributes is having many parts. So the conclusion contradicts the premise that the One is absolutely simple.
objections.reply: Feser's first answer uses Frege's **sense/reference** distinction. ‘The morning star’ and ‘the evening star’ differ in meaning but refer to one planet. Similarly, ‘the One is omnipotent’ and ‘the One is an intellect’ are not synonymous, yet both can refer to one simple reality. Different *concepts* of God are not different *components* in God. The attributes are one and the same reality, conceived or described in different ways because our finite minds must approach it from different angles.
objections.pushback: If they reply that Venus is still composite, agree: the example only shows that difference of meaning does not require difference of reality, not that Venus is simple. The simplicity comes from the argument; the Frege point merely removes the apparent contradiction.

objections.title: “But in us intellect and power really are different things”
objections.whoRaises: Sharper critics of divine simplicity (the kind of worry Alvin Plantinga develops, discussed in chapter 6)
objections.objection: Sense and reference doesn't help. In a human being, intelligence and strength aren't just two descriptions of one thing; they're genuinely distinct features — a genius can be weak, a strong man foolish. If God has intelligence and power, those are distinct features in God too.
objections.reply: Feser grants the premise about humans and concedes that the conclusion would follow *if* the terms applied to God in exactly the same sense. But precisely because the One has no parts, they should not be applied **univocally**. Following Aquinas, they are used **analogically**: not in the same sense as with us (univocal), nor in a wholly unrelated sense (equivocal, like ‘bat’), but in a related sense (like ‘good’ said of wine and of a man). To say God has power and intellect is to say there is in God something analogous to what we call power and intellect in ourselves. And one respect in which God's ‘power’ and ‘intellect’ differ from ours is exactly that in him they are one reality, whereas in us they are two. Analogical speech remains literal, not metaphorical.
objections.pushback: If the critic says analogy is a way of saying nothing, point out that we use analogical terms literally all the time (‘good’ wine, ‘good’ man; ‘healthy’ food, ‘healthy’ person) and understand them perfectly well. If they demand a full picture of how power and intellect can be identical, grant that we lack one — and turn to the next objection.

objections.title: Divine simplicity is incomprehensible, and so suspect
objections.objection: A being whose knowledge is identical to its power, which is identical to its goodness, is not something anyone can actually understand. When a conclusion is this strange, that's a sign something went wrong in the argument.
objections.reply: Feser admits the conclusion is odd, but says we should *expect* it to be. Physics offers a parallel: particles behave like both waves and particles, which no one can properly picture, yet we accept it because the evidence and reasoning demand it and because the domain is remote from everyday experience. Reasoning to the absolutely simple ground of all reality goes farther from everyday experience than physics ever does, so our concepts must stretch to their limit. It would be surprising if the result were *not* hard to grasp. Reason itself tells us there is a level of reality reason can only partly comprehend. Difficulty of comprehension is not the same as incoherence.
objections.pushback: If they say wave–particle duality is backed by experiment and this is not, reply that the analogy concerns the *expected difficulty* of concepts stretched to remote domains, not the kind of evidence. The evidence here is the argument itself; if it is sound, the strangeness must be accepted, and they should identify which premise fails.

objections.title: A further part could do the unifying
objections.whoRaises: Critics of the external-cause premise (discussed by Vallicella)
objections.objection: Why assume the cause of a thing's unity must lie outside it? Perhaps some part of the thing — a binding element, a structural principle — is what unites the other parts.
objections.reply: Following Vallicella, Feser argues that this merely relocates the problem. Suppose a thing has parts A and B, and we say part C unites them. Now we need to know what unites C with A and B. Positing a part D pushes the question back again, and so on for every new part. Instead of explaining A and B's unity, we have created more things whose unity needs explaining. A unifier that is itself one of the items to be unified cannot do the job.
objections.pushback: If the objector says C is special — a ‘relation’ rather than a thing — ask whether that relation is really distinct from A and B. If it is, the question ‘what joins the relation to its relata?’ arises again; if it isn't, then nothing has been added to explain the unity.

objections.title: The unity is just an irreducible fact about the thing
objections.whoRaises: Critics who resist the demand for explanation
objections.objection: Some facts are basic. Perhaps the fact that a thing's parts are united is simply an irreducible fact about that thing — no external cause required.
objections.reply:
Feser asks what ‘irreducible fact’ means here. Two readings are possible:

1. The composite itself causes its parts to be united. Then it would be both the cause and the effect of the same union — incoherent, a thing lifting itself by its own bootstraps.
2. The union has no cause at all; it's a brute fact. Then the critic has not given an alternative explanation, which is what he claimed to offer. He has given no explanation.

Either way, nothing has been offered that competes with the Neo-Platonic account.
objections.pushback: If they insist that brute facts are respectable in philosophy, note that this abandons the claim to have an *alternative* and moves to the next objection — the claim that maybe there is no explanation at all.

objections.title: “Maybe there's simply no explanation”
objections.whoRaises: Critics biting the bullet; defenders of brute facts
objections.objection: Fine — I have no alternative explanation. I'm simply suggesting that there may be no explanation at all of why composite things exist. That possibility is enough to block your argument.
objections.reply: As Lloyd Gerson points out, this is not a serious response to the Neo-Platonic argument. Its defender can reply: an explanation *has* been given — the parts are joined by an absolutely simple cause — and the critic has offered no reason to reject it that doesn't beg the question. Saying ‘maybe there's no explanation’ while one sits on the table is like a detective who, handed a well-supported solution, replies that perhaps the crime has no culprit. One needs a reason to reject the explanation, not merely the observation that one could refuse to explain.
objections.pushback: If they respond that the explanation is unfalsifiable or extravagant, ask what makes it so — and note that its only posit is the minimal thing any unity of parts requires: something that unites without itself needing to be united. (Chapter 5 defends the principle of sufficient reason more directly.)

objections.title: Science and the laws of nature explain composition
objections.objection: We know exactly why things hold together: electromagnetic forces bind atoms into molecules, the strong force binds quarks into protons, and so on. The laws of nature explain composition. No God required.
objections.reply:
Feser grants that such explanations are true as far as they go, but denies that they are an alternative to the argument's conclusion. Any explanation in terms of laws leaves us with a further composite. If it is a law that things of type A and type B combine under certain conditions, we must ask why A and B are governed by *that* law rather than another. A, B, and the law together form a new complex whose unity itself needs explaining — so the regress continues rather than ends.

On the Aristotelian view, laws aren't external rulers at all but summaries of how things behave given their substantial forms. That only makes things worse for the critic: substantial form is one of the two principles (with prime matter) the thing is composed of, so the working of a law presupposes the very composition it was meant to explain. However laws are construed, only something absolutely simple can end the regress.
objections.pushback: If they say the regress ends at the most fundamental law or field, ask whether that law or field has structure, several parameters, or a nature distinct from the fact that it obtains. It could have been otherwise, so it has an essence distinct from its existence. Physics describes *how* composition works at each level; the argument asks what makes the whole hierarchy of levels actual. (Chapters 7a and 7b return to laws of nature.)

objections.title: Why not stop at fundamental particles, a quantum field, or the universe itself?
objections.whoRaises: Modern naturalists; Dawkins, Krauss and others as cataloged in chapter 7 (course application)
objections.objection: Physics tells us there are fundamental particles with no smaller parts. Those are the simples. Or take the universe as a whole, or the quantum vacuum, as the ultimate uncaused reality. Why leap to God?
objections.reply: The argument's notion of a part is broader than ‘smaller physical piece.’ An electron has no smaller spatial parts, but it still has a determinate nature (mass, charge, spin) that is distinct from the fact that it exists; it has states it is in and states it could be in (actuality and potentiality); it could have failed to exist. By the chapter's own reasoning, that makes it metaphysically composite and in need of a cause. The universe is obviously composite, since it's made of all these things. A quantum field has structure, values varying across space, and a nature that could have been otherwise. Only something with no distinction whatsoever between what it is and that it is, or between what it is and what it could be, can end the regress. In chapter 7 Feser applies exactly this reasoning: the universe and a multiverse cannot be uncaused precisely because they are composite, and the laws of physics lack the required simplicity.
objections.pushback: If they deny that essence/existence or act/potency are real distinctions, recall that the argument doesn't need them for most things: physical and structural composition already rules out the universe and fields. Metaphysical parts are needed only to show that even ‘partless’ particles don't escape.

objections.title: The ‘mind’ step is a false trichotomy
objections.whoRaises: Philosophers skeptical of the attribute derivations (course application)
objections.objection: Steps 22–29 assume that everything is a mind, a mental content, a material thing, or an abstract thing. Why think that list is exhaustive? Perhaps the ultimate cause is a fifth kind of thing we cannot categorize. And minds, as we know them, are complex — how could something utterly simple think?
objections.reply: Feser flags the modesty of the conclusion: following Vallicella, the One is ‘either a mind, or more like a mind than anything else.’ So the elimination does not claim to picture a divine mind; it locates the One nearer to mind than to any other category we know. That fits the analogical account: divine intellect is not a human-style process with parts but something analogous to it. The inference is also reinforced by chapter 1's argument from proportionate causality, carried over in step 35: a cause must in some way possess what it produces, and intellect is among the things the One produces. Chapter 6 develops divine intellect at length. Note, too, that Plotinus himself denied intellect to the One — so this is a point where Feser consciously revises the tradition he borrows from.
objections.pushback: If they propose a mysterious fifth category, ask what it would be like: if it causes, it isn't inert like an abstraction; if it is partless, it isn't material; if it is ultimate, it isn't a dependent thought. Whatever it is, it must possess, in a higher way, whatever is found in its effects — including thought. That is all ‘more like a mind than anything else’ claims.

objections.title: A partless being would be empty — or an abstract property
objections.whoRaises: Alvin Plantinga and other theistic personalists (answered in chapter 6)
objections.objection: If God is identical to each of his attributes, then all his attributes are identical to one another, and God is just one property. But properties are abstract objects. So divine simplicity turns God into an abstract object — or, if he has no properties, into a featureless blank.
objections.reply: Feser answers Plantinga in chapter 6, but the key moves are already present in chapter 2. First, simplicity is not emptiness: the One is *purely actual*, the fullness of being with no unrealized potential, not a bare something with nothing to it. Second, the objection interprets ‘power’, ‘knowledge’ and ‘property’ univocally, as if God had them in the same way we do and as if properties were Platonic abstract objects. Classical theists reject both assumptions; attributes are predicated analogically, and God is never said to be a ‘property’ at all. Third, this chapter itself argues that the One cannot be an abstract entity, since abstractions are causally inert and the One is the cause of everything.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘then I don't understand what simplicity means,’ return to the positive content: no parts, no potentiality, no dependence. Everything we know about composite things tells us what God is *not*; the analogical terms tell us what in God corresponds, in a higher way, to perfections in creatures.

misconceptions.myth: The Neo-Platonic proof argues that the universe must have had a beginning.
misconceptions.correction: It is indifferent to whether the universe had a beginning. The dependence of a composite on its parts is atemporal, holding at each moment; the regress is traced down to a present sustaining cause, not back to a first moment.

misconceptions.myth: The argument rests on the premise that everything has a cause.
misconceptions.correction: Its premise is that whatever is composite has a cause of its composition. Something absolutely simple not only needs no cause but could not have one — so God is not a special-pleading exception.

misconceptions.myth: ‘Simple’ means primitive, empty, or easy to understand.
misconceptions.correction: It means partless. The One is the fullness of actuality with no parts, potentials, or limits — and Feser stresses that it is very hard to understand, as we should expect.

misconceptions.myth: Being immaterial is the same as being simple, so a soul or an angel could be the One.
misconceptions.correction: Absolute simplicity rules out metaphysical composition too (form/matter, essence/existence, act/potency, bearer/feature). An immaterial creature still has an essence distinct from its existence, so it is composite and caused.

misconceptions.myth: You must accept Aristotelian form and matter or Thomistic essence and existence for the argument to work.
misconceptions.correction: Feser says explicitly that nothing rides on those theories. The principle ‘whatever is composite has a cause’ is completely general and works with ordinary physical parts. The metaphysical parts simply show how far the principle reaches.

misconceptions.myth: Feser's proof is just Plotinus's system, so accepting it commits you to emanation and to intellect being below the One.
misconceptions.correction: Feser adopts the general Neo-Platonic strategy — from composition to an absolutely simple source — and departs from Plotinus by concluding that the One is itself a mind, as later thinkers like Augustine and Aquinas did.

misconceptions.myth: If God's attributes are spoken of analogically, then talk about God is merely metaphorical.
misconceptions.correction: Analogical predication is literal. Wine and George are both literally good, in related but different senses. God is literally powerful and wise, in a sense analogous to, not identical with, ours.

misconceptions.myth: The One and the Unmoved Mover are two different ultimate beings reached by two different proofs.
misconceptions.correction: Both are purely actual, and there can only be one purely actual being, so they are the same reality. The two proofs are different routes (parts/whole vs. act/potency) to the same summit.

misconceptions.myth: The regress must end simply because infinite chains are impossible.
misconceptions.correction: The point is the hierarchical character of the series: every member has only borrowed ‘holding-together’ power, so without an unborrowed source there would be none at all. A linear series (like a line of chair-makers) is not what the argument says must terminate.
